title: Japan Protests China's Live-Fire Naval Drill in Disputed Pacific Waters
excerpt: Tokyo lodges formal diplomatic protest after a Chinese guided-missile destroyer conducted a live-fire exercise near Japan's southernmost atoll, marking the first such public disclosure of Chinese military drills in Japan's exclusive economic zone.
body:
• Japan lodged a formal diplomatic protest with Beijing after a Chinese guided-missile destroyer carried out a live-fire drill 180 km southwest of Okinotorishima on Sunday.
  • This marks the first time Tokyo has publicly disclosed Chinese live-fire exercises in its claimed exclusive economic zone.
  • The drill involved a four-vessel flotilla including two Chinese destroyers and a Russian frigate, following a week of joint Sino-Russian naval exercises near Qingdao.
  • China rejected Japan's protest, calling it "completely unreasonable" and insisting its activities comply with international law.

Japan on Tuesday lodged a formal diplomatic protest with China after a Chinese guided-missile destroyer carried out a live-fire drill in waters near the country's southernmost atoll, escalating maritime tensions between Asia's two largest economies.

A Renhai-class guided-missile destroyer conducted the exercise early Sunday approximately 180 km (110 miles) southwest of Okinotorishima, an uninhabited coral atoll in the Philippine Sea between Taiwan and Guam, according to Japan's Defense Ministry. The destroyer was part of a four-vessel flotilla that included a second Chinese guided-missile destroyer, a Fuchi-class replenishment ship, and a Russian Steregushchiy-class frigate.

"The Japanese government lodged a protest with China through diplomatic channels, on the grounds that such activities could pose a danger to the navigation of nearby vessels."

— Minoru Kihara, Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary

Japanese forces said Chinese forces announced the drill by radio shortly before it was carried out, according to Kihara. A spokesperson for Japan's military confirmed this was the first time Tokyo had publicly disclosed live-fire drills by China within its claimed exclusive economic zone.

The Okinotorishima Dispute

The incident is rooted in a long-running disagreement over the status of Okinotorishima. Japan claims the feature as an island, which entitles it to an exclusive economic zone of more than 154,000 square miles — an area larger than Japan's total land mass. China argues the feature is a rock or reef, not an island, and therefore does not generate an EEZ under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

China's Foreign Ministry rejected Japan's protest. Spokesperson Lin Jian called Tokyo's concerns "completely unreasonable" during a Tuesday press conference, saying "China's activities on the high seas are in line with international law and practices" and accusing Japan of "smearing and hyping up the legitimate actions of other countries."

Escalating Sino-Russian Naval Cooperation

The drill came days after China and Russia concluded a week-long joint naval exercise in waters off Qingdao, eastern China. Senior Colonel Jiang Bin, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of National Defense, said those exercises "played an important role in safeguarding the sovereignty and security" of both countries and did not target any third party.

China and Russia have carried out increasingly complex and assertive joint military operations near Japan in recent years. Tokyo has responded by increasing surveillance and strengthening defenses across its archipelago. In December, Japan accused Chinese fighter jets of aiming their radar at Japanese military aircraft near Okinawa, an account Beijing disputed.

Fraying Relations Between Tokyo and Beijing

The episode adds to already strained ties. Relations deteriorated after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested in November that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could force Japan to mobilize its military. Beijing was incensed by the remarks, advising its citizens to avoid Japan and imposing trade restrictions.

Japan's own military posture has shifted. During the Balikatan joint exercises with the United States and the Philippines in May, Japan fired Type 88 anti-ship missiles overseas for the first time since World War II. Beijing condemned the test as evidence of "accelerated remilitarization."

Implications for India and the Indo-Pacific

For India, Japan's growing maritime tensions with China underscore shared security concerns across the Indo-Pacific. India and Japan are both members of the Quad — the security grouping that also includes the United States and Australia — and have deepened bilateral defense ties in recent years. The two countries conduct regular Malabar naval exercises and have expanded cooperation on maritime domain awareness.

China's assertion that Okinotorishima does not warrant an EEZ has parallels with territorial disputes in the South China Sea, where Beijing's expansive maritime claims challenge those of several Southeast Asian nations. For Indian strategists, the pattern of Chinese naval assertiveness — from the Indian Ocean to the Western Pacific — reinforces the case for a coordinated Indo-Pacific security architecture.

What's Next

Analysts expect the Okinotorishima EEZ dispute and broader Sino-Japanese maritime tensions to remain a flashpoint. While China and Russia's joint naval cooperation shows growing sophistication, analysts at the Wall Street Journal noted that it still does not match the degree of integration seen in exercises involving the U.S. and its allies. Tokyo is likely to continue publicly disclosing Chinese military activities in the area — a departure from Japan's traditionally discreet approach — as part of a broader strategy to build international pressure on Beijing's maritime assertiveness.
